Craig Voorhees, 48, a workers’ compensation lawyer, commutes 40 minutes to Somerville, N.J. Ms. Voorhees, 46, an artist, walks down the hill to her studio in Lambertville’s business district.
Seven years ago, she was offered art studio space at the People’s Store Antiques and Design Center, a 180-year-old building on North Union Street with more than 50 vendors peddling collectibles. Climb to the third floor, and you’ll likely find her among her urban streetscapes and rural landscapes, ready to lay down her paintbrush and schmooze.
Lambertville, she said, is a place of “free spirits, and you want to be around that feeling.”
Half a century ago, Lambertville was largely blue-collar, with ragged buildings and industries. In the 1970s, it began to capitalize on its vintage charm and proximity to New York City and Philadelphia. Preservation-minded settlers bought and renovated the old houses. Rago Auctions, which opened in 1994 in a former silk-hosiery mill on North Main Street, was one of the anchors of that transformation. (Rago recently merged with the Chicago auction house Wright, but will remain in place.)
“When my wife and I moved to Lambertville 30-something years ago, all the homes were a fixer-upper, and we met all our friends at the local hardware store and lumberyard,” said Bradley Sanford, an agent with River Valley Realty’s Lambertville office. Now, with renovations completed and buyers interested in turnkey properties, such meetings occur “not so much,” he said.
Mr. Sanford, 60, described today’s Lambertville in the most complimentary way, as a “Disneyesque town completely populated by Dickens characters.” More than once, he has noticed residents carrying bags around to scoop up litter on their afternoon strolls. The city, he said, is a haven for boaters who paddle on the river, and has “the world’s coolest Elks lodge.”
Lambertville also trades energy with nearby river towns like Stockton and Frenchtown, in New Jersey, and is just a footbridge away from New Hope, Pa., with its art galleries, fine restaurants and
regional theater
. (Ms. Voorhees described the mirroring as “two towns for the price of one.”)
While daily long-distance commuting is not common, many residents travel multiple times a week to jobs in New York City or Pennsylvania. April Lindner, 57, drives a bit more than an hour, off peak, to Philadelphia, where she teaches creative writing and poetry at Saint Joseph’s University up to four days a week.
She and her husband, André St. Amant, 56, a territory manager for a hardware company, bolted from the Philadelphia suburbs for Lambertville three years ago, after their youngest child left for college. They paid $325,000 for a newly remodeled 1880s farmhouse-style building on Route 518. The property has three bedrooms, a sewing porch and a painting studio. “We see hawks and an occasional bald eagle and sometimes vultures,” Ms. Lindner said. “We feel like we’re very close to the natural world.”
Lambertville is also popular with weekenders. Six years ago,
Margey Peters and Brad Vickers
, musicians and visual artists based in Manhattan, spent $600,000 on a 1988 post-and-beam house on Cottage Hill, with three-season views of the river. Ms. Peters said the house was exactly like one she dreamed of as a child: “We didn’t even look around and compare properties.”
Julia Fahl, 29, also moved to Lambertville after falling in love — not with the city but with Kari Osmond, now her wife, a deputy chief of staff for a United States representative. Mrs. Fahl, a political campaign fund-raiser, thought the city needed new leadership and sought a replacement for its mayoral incumbent, David DelVecchio, who had been in office since she was an infant. After failing to recruit anyone to challenge him in the Democratic primary, she did it herself and won, then ran unopposed in the general election last year. In her first eight months as mayor, she completed a road-improvement project that she said had been on hold for 18 years.
“We have not been without our issues and concerns,” Mrs. Fahl noted, including the “evergreen” problem of where to park when the tourists hit town, and a ballooning budget deficit that will require the city to find between $2.5 million and $4 million in revenue by 2025 (the current budget is $5.3 million).

One strategy is to attract technology and innovation companies to Lambertville. “The city is already chock-full of charm,” Mrs. Fahl said. Now it is poised to use that charm to “encourage not just retail sales but business development.”
What You’ll Find
Lambertville covers 1.1 square miles in southwestern Hunterdon County and has a population of about 3,800 residents. According to 2017 American Community Survey data, 92.9 percent of the community is white, 2.7 percent Hispanic or Latino, 2.3 percent black or African-American and 1.7 percent Asian.
The city’s business district is concentrated for several blocks along the Delaware River and east to Route 29. Single-family houses and a few townhouse communities are north and south of downtown. Properties rise up the slopes of Cottage Hill, Connaught Hill and Lambert’s Hill (formerly known as Music Mountain, and the site of a development with large houses built from 2004 to 2008).
The majority of the 2,200 housing units are in buildings that predate 1900, both minimally adorned neo-Classical residences built before the mid 19th century and the gussied-up Victorians that followed — or the two combined. (Mr. Sanford suspects that one of his listings, a brick house on Weeden Street purportedly built in the 1860s, is 1830s at its core. Such layering is not uncommon, he said.)
More than 40 percent of those who live in Lambertville rent
, and the market for one-bedrooms is competitive. The units are mostly in multifamily houses and, to a lesser extent, above shops in the business district.
It is to Lambertville’s credit that you can ask half a dozen residents to name their favorite haunts, and find few overlaps. Opinions converge on the Delaware and Raritan Canal path, a portion of which stretches alongside the river all the way to Trenton, 16 miles away, and is enjoyed by cyclists and pedestrians (and their dogs). Multiple mentions are also made of the bar at Anton’s at the Swan restaurant, the Mexican-Peruvian El Tule restaurant, and Lambertville House hotel and restaurant, in a building constructed in 1812 for Captain John Lambert, a member of the city’s namesake family. (This is not to be confused with Lambertville Station Restaurant and Inn, in a 19th-century railroad depot.)
Votes are also cast for home-décor shops like Blue Raccoon, cafes like Bucks on the Bridge (and the J.B. Kline vintage music instrument shop above it) and construction-supply stores like the 102-year-old Finkles. Praise is showered on the independent character of Lambertville businesses in general — not even a Starbucks, which is more than New Hope can claim. But one downside to living in a tourist-facing city, residents say, is the shortage of supermarkets.
“You have to go to the Giant in New Hope,” Ms. Peters said. “In Lambertville, there’s the City Market,” which is more of a convenience store. (A Basil Bandwagon Natural Market is slated to arrive soon on North Union Street.)
Lambertville pulls locals and visitors alike to Shad Fest, a two-day festival held during the last week of April, with contributions from musicians, artists and chefs. On Oct. 20, the Lambertville Historical Society will hold its 37th annual house-tour benefit. The city also attracts outsiders to its blowout Halloween celebrations, including a parade scheduled for Oct. 27.
What You’ll Pay
According to Realtor.com, the median sale price of Lambertville homes in August was $451,000, a year-over-year increase of 5.8 percent. Properties remained on the market for a median of 78 days, a decrease of 8.2 percent from the previous year.
Zillow showed a 2.2 percent decline in median home values in Lambertville in the year preceding Aug. 31, and predicted that values will fall an additional 0.9 percent in the next year. Rentals average around $2,300 a month.
As of Sept. 30, 42 properties in good condition, drawn from multiple listing sources, were on Trulia’s website. They ranged from a two-bedroom, one-bathroom frame house on Route 179, built in 1920 and priced at $229,000, with taxes of $3,774, to a three-bedroom, five-bathroom home built last year in an old machine shop on York Street and priced at $994,500, with taxes of $24,470.
“This is New Jersey, so the taxes are high, but not as high as in other areas,” said Erin McManus-Keyes, an agent with Hunterdon Bucks Realty in Lambertville and the city’s fire department commissioner. She volunteered her own recent tax bill as an example: $10,000 on a house assessed at $480,000, of which $6,000 were school taxes.
The Vibe
Lambertville is a continual buffet of cultural and social opportunities. On a recent evening, Vincent Uhl, a hydrogeologist and a longtime resident, was walking along Coryell Street with his wife and professional partner, Jaclyn Baron, when he saw an open door, bottles of wine and a familiar face. He stepped into what he thought was a gallery opening. It was actually a women’s book group. He might have hung around, but he was escorting Ms. Baron to her own women’s book group down the street.
The Schools
The South Hunterdon Regional School District serves the communities of Lambertville, Stockton and West Amwell with two elementary schools, in Lambertville and West Amwell, and a combined middle school and high school in West Amwell.
In the 2017-18 school year, the Lambertville Public School enrolled 251 students in prekindergarten through sixth grade. Among the students who took state tests that year, 47.4 met standards in English versus 58.7 percent districtwide, and 42.6 percent met standards in math versus 39.4 percent districtwide. Although the Board of Education has floated the idea of moving the school from its convenient location on North Main Street to West Amwell, Mrs. Fahl said the Lambertville community “really stands behind the idea of having a walking school district.”
South Hunterdon Regional High School enrolls about 450 students in seventh through 12th grade. Average SAT scores for the class of 2018 were 565 in reading and writing and 559 in math, versus 542 and 543 statewide.
The Commute
Trans-Bridge Lines offers bus service from Lambertville to Port Authority, Newark Liberty International Airport and Kennedy International Airport. Travel time to Port Authority is an hour and 45 minutes, and the round-trip fare is $28. New Jersey Transit train service is available on the Northeast Corridor Line from Trenton, as well as from Hamilton, N.J., about 20 miles southeast. Amtrak serves Trenton as well.
The History
Lambertville’s industrial heyday began typically, with the arrival of the railroad in 1851, and yielded some of the fancier Italianate and French Empire-style Victorians on the north side of the city. The local factories made spokes (and eventually whole wheels), “snag-proof” rubber boots, porcelain toilet bowls and tanks, and at the turn of the 20th century, 15 tons of hairpins a week.
